title: November Examination: Paper 2
instructions: This question paper consists of 9 questions. Answer ALL the questions.
Clearly show ALL calculations, diagrams, graphs, et cetera that you have used in determining your answers. Answers only will NOT necessarily be awarded full marks.
You may use an approved scientific calculator (non-programmable and non-graphical), unless stated otherwise.
If necessary, round off answers to TWO decimal places, unless stated otherwise.
Diagrams are NOT necessarily drawn to scale.
In Euclidean geometry, every statement must be supported by a reason.
An information sheet with formulae is given at the start of QUESTION 1.

In this app: type a final answer in the answer box where one is given. For written questions, do the full working on paper first, then compare with the memo and award yourself the marks shown by the ticks (✓).

context.text:
The times (in minutes) that 15 Grade 10 learners from a school in Polokwane took to travel to school one morning are given below:

36 ; 24 ; 41 ; 12 ; 35 ; 30 ; 38 ; 27 ; 36 ; 40 ; 20 ; 34 ; 39 ; 32 ; 36

context.caption: Distance run in one week by the 40 members of a running club in Durban

questions.prompt: Calculate the mean travel time of the 15 learners. Give your answer correct to two decimal places where necessary.
questions.explanation: The sum of the 15 times is $480$, so the mean is $\dfrac{480}{15} = 32$ minutes.

questions.prompt: Determine the median travel time.
Write down the mode of the travel times.
questions.explanation: $36$ occurs three times, more often than any other value.

questions.prompt: Determine the lower quartile ($Q_1$) of the travel times.
questions.explanation: $Q_1$ is the median of the 7 values below the median (12 ; 20 ; 24 ; 27 ; 30 ; 32 ; 34), i.e. the 4th value: $27$.

questions.prompt: Determine the upper quartile ($Q_3$) of the travel times.
questions.explanation: $Q_3$ is the median of the 7 values above the median (36 ; 36 ; 36 ; 38 ; 39 ; 40 ; 41), i.e. the 12th value overall: $38$.

questions.prompt: Calculate the interquartile range (IQR) of the travel times.
questions.explanation: $\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1 = 38 - 27 = 11$ minutes.

questions.prompt: Write down the five-number summary of the travel times and use it to draw a box-and-whisker diagram on a number line.
questions.memo:
Five-number summary: minimum $12$ ; $Q_1 = 27$ ; median $35$ ; $Q_3 = 38$ ; maximum $41$

✓ whiskers drawn from 12 to 27 and from 38 to 41 (1)
✓ box drawn from 27 to 38 with the median line at 35 (1)

(A correct, roughly scaled number line is expected.)

questions.prompt: Use your box-and-whisker diagram and the mean to describe the skewness of the data. Give a reason for your answer.
questions.memo:
✓ The data is negatively skewed (skewed to the left), because the mean ($32$) is less than the median ($35$) / the left whisker (12 to 27) is much longer than the right whisker (38 to 41) / the median is closer to $Q_3$ than to $Q_1$. (1)

(The mark is awarded only for the correct skewness WITH a valid reason.)

questions.prompt: Use the frequency table to calculate the estimated mean distance run by the members of the running club. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.
Write down the modal class of the distances run.
questions.explanation: The modal class is the class with the highest frequency: $10 \leq x < 20$ has 14 members.

questions.prompt: In which class does the median distance lie?
questions.explanation: With 40 members the median lies between the 20th and 21st values. The cumulative frequencies are 4 ; 18 ; 29 ; 36 ; 40, so the 20th and 21st values both lie in $20 \leq x < 30$.

questions.prompt: Calculate the length of AB.
Calculate the gradient of AC. Give your answer as a common fraction (e.g. 2/5) or as a decimal correct to two decimal places.
Determine the equation of the line AC in the form $y = mx + c$.
questions.memo:
$m_{AC} = \dfrac{1}{3}$ ✓ (1)
Substitute $A(-2; 1)$: $1 = \dfrac{1}{3}(-2) + c$ ✓ (1)
$c = \dfrac{5}{3}$, so $y = \dfrac{1}{3}x + \dfrac{5}{3}$ ✓ (1)

(Alternative: $y - 1 = \dfrac{1}{3}(x + 2)$ earns the same marks once simplified to $y = \dfrac{1}{3}x + \dfrac{5}{3}$.)

questions.prompt: Determine the coordinates of M, the midpoint of AC.
ABCD is a parallelogram. Use the fact that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other to determine the coordinates of D.
questions.memo:
M is also the midpoint of BD:
$\dfrac{2 + x_D}{2} = \dfrac{5}{2}$, so $x_D = 3$ ✓ (1)
$\dfrac{4 + y_D}{2} = \dfrac{5}{2}$, so $y_D = 1$ ✓ (1)

$D(3; 1)$

(Alternative: the translation from B to A is (x − 4; y − 3), so D = C(7; 4) moved the same way = (3; 1).)

questions.prompt: Prove that parallelogram ABCD is a rhombus.
questions.memo:
Method 1 (diagonals):
$m_{BD} = \dfrac{4 - 1}{2 - 3} = -3$ ✓ (1)
$m_{AC} \times m_{BD} = \dfrac{1}{3} \times (-3) = -1$ ✓ (1)
$\therefore AC \perp BD$ ✓ (1)
ABCD is a parallelogram with perpendicular diagonals, so ABCD is a rhombus ✓ (1)

Method 2 (adjacent sides):
$AB = 5$ (from 2.1) ✓ (1)
$AD = \sqrt{(3 - (-2))^2 + (1 - 1)^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5$ ✓✓ (2)
ABCD is a parallelogram with a pair of adjacent sides equal ($AB = AD$), so ABCD is a rhombus ✓ (1)

questions.prompt: Use a calculator to evaluate, correct to two decimal places: $\cos 52^\circ + \sin 38^\circ$
questions.explanation: $\cos 52^\circ + \sin 38^\circ = 0{,}6157 + 0{,}6157 = 1{,}2313... \approx 1{,}23$ (make sure the calculator is in degree mode).

questions.prompt: Use a calculator to evaluate, correct to two decimal places: $\dfrac{\tan 65^\circ}{2\sin 25^\circ}$
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{2{,}1445...}{2 \times 0{,}4226...} = 2{,}5371... \approx 2{,}54$. Put the whole denominator in brackets on the calculator.

questions.prompt: Use a calculator to evaluate, correct to two decimal places: $\sec 40^\circ$
Without using a calculator, determine the value of $\dfrac{\sin 60^\circ \cdot \tan 30^\circ}{\cos^2 45^\circ}$.
questions.memo:
$= \dfrac{\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}{\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2}$
✓ $\sin 60^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ (1)
✓ $\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ (1)
✓ $\cos^2 45^\circ = \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}$ (1)
$= \dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{\frac{1}{2}} = 1$ ✓ (1)

questions.prompt: Solve for $\theta$, where $0^\circ \leq \theta \leq 90^\circ$: $3\sin\theta = 2$. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: $\sin\theta = \dfrac{2}{3}$, so $\theta = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right) = 41{,}81^\circ$.

questions.prompt: Solve for $\theta$, where $0^\circ \leq \theta \leq 90^\circ$: $2\cos(\theta + 15^\circ) = 0{,}8$. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: $\cos(\theta + 15^\circ) = 0{,}4$, so $\theta + 15^\circ = \cos^{-1}(0{,}4) = 66{,}42^\circ$. Therefore $\theta = 66{,}42^\circ - 15^\circ = 51{,}42^\circ$.

questions.prompt: Refer to $\triangle PQR$. Without calculating the size of any angle, determine the value of $\sin R + \cos R$.
Refer to $\triangle PQR$. Calculate the size of $\hat{R}$, correct to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: $\tan R = \dfrac{\text{opp}}{\text{adj}} = \dfrac{PQ}{QR} = \dfrac{8}{15}$, so $\hat{R} = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{8}{15}\right) = 28{,}07^\circ$.

sections.title: QUESTION 4: Trigonometry on the Cartesian Plane
sections.instructions: Answer this question WITHOUT using a calculator. Draw sketches on the Cartesian plane where needed.

questions.prompt: Given: $13\cos\theta - 5 = 0$ and $\sin\theta < 0$. Use a sketch to determine the value of $\sin\theta$.
questions.memo:
$\cos\theta = \dfrac{5}{13}$, so $x = 5$ and $r = 13$, with $\theta$ in the fourth quadrant ($\cos\theta > 0$, $\sin\theta < 0$) ✓ (1)
$y^2 = 13^2 - 5^2 = 144$, so $y = -12$ (negative in the fourth quadrant) ✓ (1)
$\sin\theta = \dfrac{y}{r} = -\dfrac{12}{13}$ ✓ (1)

questions.prompt: Hence, determine the value of $\tan\theta + \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}$.
questions.memo:
$\tan\theta = \dfrac{y}{x} = -\dfrac{12}{5}$ ✓ (1)
$\tan\theta + \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} = -\dfrac{12}{5} + \dfrac{13}{5} = \dfrac{1}{5}$ ✓ (1)

questions.prompt: The point $P(-2; k)$ lies on the terminal arm of angle $\beta$ in standard position, with $OP = \sqrt{13}$ and $180^\circ < \beta < 270^\circ$. Determine the value of $k$ and hence the value of $\cos\beta$.
questions.memo:
$(-2)^2 + k^2 = (\sqrt{13})^2$ ✓ (1)
$k^2 = 9$, and $k < 0$ because $\beta$ is in the third quadrant, so $k = -3$ ✓ (1)
$\cos\beta = \dfrac{x}{r} = -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}}$ $\left(= -\dfrac{2\sqrt{13}}{13}\right)$ ✓ (1)

context.text: The graphs of $f(x) = a\sin x + q$ (solid line) and $g(x) = 2\cos x + 1$ (dashed line) are sketched below for $0^\circ \leq x \leq 360^\circ$. The maximum point of $f$ is $(90^\circ; 3)$ and its minimum point is $(270^\circ; -1)$. The two graphs intersect where $x = 45^\circ$ and $x = 225^\circ$.

questions.prompt: Write down the value of $a$.
questions.explanation: The amplitude of $f$ is $\dfrac{3 - (-1)}{2} = 2$. The graph has the shape of $y = \sin x$ (it rises from $x = 0^\circ$ to a maximum at $90^\circ$), so $a = 2$.

questions.prompt: Write down the value of $q$.
questions.explanation: The graph is shifted up so that its centre line is halfway between 3 and −1: $q = \dfrac{3 + (-1)}{2} = 1$.

questions.prompt: Write down the amplitude of $g$.
questions.explanation: For $y = a\cos x + q$ the amplitude is $|a|$, so the amplitude of $g$ is $2$.

questions.prompt: Write down the period of $g$.
questions.explanation: The graph of $y = a\cos x + q$ completes one full cycle every $360^\circ$.

questions.prompt: Write down the range of $g$.
questions.memo:
$-1 \leq y \leq 3$ ✓✓ (2)
(or $y \in [-1; 3]$)

✓ for each correct end value with the correct inequality signs; a maximum of 1 mark if strict inequalities ($<$) are used.

Use the graphs to determine the values of $x$, for $0^\circ \leq x \leq 360^\circ$, for which $f(x) > g(x)$.
questions.memo:

Sipho stands at C, further from the mast, so that B, A and C lie in a straight line. The angle of elevation of T from C is $22^\circ$.

questions.prompt: Calculate the height of the mast, TB, correct to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: In right-angled $\triangle TBA$: $\tan 35^\circ = \dfrac{TB}{40}$, so $TB = 40\tan 35^\circ = 28{,}01$ m.

questions.prompt: Calculate the distance AC between Lerato and Sipho.
questions.memo:
In $\triangle TBC$: $\tan 22^\circ = \dfrac{TB}{BC}$ ✓ (1)
$BC = \dfrac{28{,}01}{\tan 22^\circ} = 69{,}32$ m ✓ (1)
$AC = BC - AB = 69{,}32 - 40 = 29{,}32$ m ✓ (1)

(Accept 29,32 m or 29,33 m, depending on rounding of TB.)

questions.prompt: Calculate the distance CT from Sipho to the top of the mast, correct to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: $\sin 22^\circ = \dfrac{TB}{CT}$, so $CT = \dfrac{28{,}01}{\sin 22^\circ} = 74{,}77$ m. (Pythagoras with $BC = 69{,}32$ m gives the same answer.)

questions.prompt: Name the quadrilateral that has exactly one pair of opposite angles equal and diagonals that intersect at right angles.
questions.explanation: A kite has two pairs of equal adjacent sides; its diagonals are perpendicular and only the pair of angles between the unequal sides is equal.

questions.prompt: Complete the statement: If both pairs of opposite angles of a quadrilateral are equal, then the quadrilateral is a ...
questions.explanation: This is one of the tests for a parallelogram (converse of the property that opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal).

questions.prompt: Write down the size of $A\hat{E}B$. Give a reason.
questions.memo: $A\hat{E}B = 90^\circ$ (diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular) ✓ S/R (1)

questions.prompt: Calculate, with reasons, the size of $B\hat{A}C$.
questions.memo:
In $\triangle ABE$:
$B\hat{A}C = 180^\circ - (90^\circ + 28^\circ) = 62^\circ$ ✓ S (1)
(sum of the angles of a triangle) ✓ R (1)

questions.prompt: Calculate, with reasons, the size of $A\hat{D}C$.
questions.memo:
$A\hat{D}B = A\hat{B}D = 28^\circ$ (angles opposite equal sides; $AB = AD$, sides of a rhombus) ✓ S/R (1)
$B\hat{D}C = A\hat{B}D = 28^\circ$ (alternate angles; $AB \parallel DC$) ✓ S/R (1)
$A\hat{D}C = 28^\circ + 28^\circ = 56^\circ$ ✓ (1)

Alternative:
$A\hat{B}C = 2 \times 28^\circ = 56^\circ$ (diagonal bisects the angles of a rhombus) ✓✓ S/R (2)
$A\hat{D}C = A\hat{B}C = 56^\circ$ (opposite angles of a parallelogram) ✓ (1)

questions.prompt: Refer to the diagram of parallelogram PQRS. Prove that PKRL is a parallelogram.
questions.memo:
$PO = OR$ (diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other) ✓ S/R (1)
$QO = OS$ (diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other) ✓ S/R (1)
$QK = SL$ (given), so $QO - QK = OS - SL$, i.e. $KO = OL$ ✓ S (1)
$\therefore$ PKRL is a parallelogram (diagonals bisect each other) ✓ R (1)

Alternative (congruency): In $\triangle PQK$ and $\triangle RSL$: $PQ = RS$ (opp sides of parallelogram), $P\hat{Q}K = R\hat{S}L$ (alt angles, $PQ \parallel SR$), $QK = SL$ (given), so $\triangle PQK \equiv \triangle RSL$ (SAS) ✓ and $PK = RL$ ✓. Similarly $\triangle PSL \equiv \triangle RQK$ (SAS), so $PL = RK$ ✓. Both pairs of opposite sides are equal, so PKRL is a parallelogram ✓.

questions.prompt: State the midpoint theorem.
questions.memo: The line segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle ✓ (1) is parallel to the third side and equal to half the length of the third side ✓ (1).

questions.prompt: Prove that PQRS is a parallelogram.
questions.memo:
In $\triangle ABC$: $PQ \parallel AC$ and $PQ = \dfrac{1}{2}AC$ (midpoint theorem) ✓ S/R (1)
In $\triangle ADC$: $SR \parallel AC$ and $SR = \dfrac{1}{2}AC$ (midpoint theorem) ✓ S/R (1)
$\therefore PQ \parallel SR$ and $PQ = SR$ ✓ S (1)
$\therefore$ PQRS is a parallelogram (one pair of opposite sides equal and parallel) ✓ R (1)

(Also accept: using $\triangle ABD$ and $\triangle CBD$ to show $PS \parallel QR$ and $PS = QR$, or showing both pairs of opposite sides parallel.)

questions.prompt: If $AC = 18$ cm and $BD = 12$ cm, calculate the perimeter of PQRS.
questions.explanation: By the midpoint theorem $PQ = SR = \dfrac{1}{2}AC = 9$ cm and $PS = QR = \dfrac{1}{2}BD = 6$ cm. Perimeter $= 2(9 + 6) = 30$ cm.

context.text:
A farmer in the Free State stores maize in a closed silo made up of a right circular cylinder with a right circular cone on top. The cylinder and the cone both have a radius of 3 m. The height of the cylinder is 5 m and the perpendicular height of the cone is 4 m. The silo stands on a concrete slab, so its base is not exposed.

Use the formulae on the information sheet (QUESTION 1) and the $\pi$ key on your calculator.

questions.prompt: Calculate the slant height of the cone.
Calculate the volume of the silo, correct to two decimal places.
Calculate the exposed outer surface area of the silo (the curved surface of the cylinder and the curved surface of the cone; the base is not included), correct to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: Curved surface of cylinder: $2\pi r h = 2\pi(3)(5) = 30\pi$. Curved surface of cone: $\pi r s = \pi(3)(5) = 15\pi$. Total $= 45\pi = 141{,}37\ \text{m}^2$. (Do not include the circle where the cone meets the cylinder; it is inside the silo.)

questions.prompt: The farmer builds a larger silo of the same shape by multiplying the radius, the height of the cylinder and the perpendicular height of the cone each by 3. Show that the volume of the larger silo is 27 times the volume of the original silo.
questions.memo:
$V_{\text{new}} = \pi(3r)^2(3h) + \dfrac{1}{3}\pi(3r)^2(3H)$ ✓ (1)
$= 27\pi r^2 h + 27 \cdot \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 H = 27\left(\pi r^2 h + \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 H\right) = 27V$ ✓ (1)

(Also accept a numerical check: $V_{\text{new}} = \pi(9)^2(15) + \dfrac{1}{3}\pi(9)^2(12) = 1\,215\pi + 324\pi = 1\,539\pi = 27 \times 57\pi$.)

questions.prompt: By what factor is the exposed outer surface area multiplied when all the dimensions are multiplied by 3?
questions.explanation: Every area is the product of two lengths, and each length (including the slant height) is multiplied by 3, so the area is multiplied by $3^2 = 9$: $45\pi \to 405\pi$.
